title: Do You Need a Data Scientist to Run an AI Feedback Analytics Platform?
summary: No. On a platform you buy, the operator is an insights analyst or CX manager, not a data scientist. Here is what each of the four jobs actually requires.
body_markdown:
This question almost always arrives the same way. A CX or insights team finds a platform it wants. Someone in the approval chain asks whether the team can actually operate it. Nobody has a data scientist to spare, and the project stalls there rather than on price.


The short answer is no. The reason is that "running the platform" is four different jobs bundled into one word: standing it up, operating it week to week, interpreting what it says, and keeping it accurate as customers change how they talk. Those have different skill requirements. On a platform you buy, two belong to the vendor, one needs an analyst, and one needs somebody who knows your business. None of them needs a data scientist.


Here's what each of those four jobs requires, who actually sits in the seat, what a data scientist would cost you if you hired one anyway, and the three cases where you genuinely do want one.


## What does "running the platform" actually mean?


The word hides four jobs. Separating them is most of the answer.


- **Standing it up.** Connecting data sources, mapping columns, getting a first analysis. On a bought platform this is a scoped implementation, not a project.
- **Operating it.** Running analyses, building views, answering questions from other teams, sending reports out.
- **Interpreting it.** Deciding what a theme means for your business, which movement matters, and what to do about it.
- **Keeping it accurate.** Making sure the themes still fit as customer language changes.


Build your own system and all four are yours, with the fourth never ending. Buy one and the first is scoped and time-boxed, the fourth belongs to the vendor, and what's left is operating and interpreting. Those are analyst jobs.


Two of these have their own answers worth reading if they're your actual question.[Whether the AI needs training on your data](https://getthematic.com/insights/does-feedback-analytics-ai-need-training) covers standing it up.[Whether the themes need manual tuning](https://getthematic.com/insights/does-thematic-require-manual-theme-tuning) covers keeping it accurate. This piece is about the person in the seat.


## Who actually sits in the seat?


Not a data scientist. In Thematic's published customer work, the operators are an insights analyst, a research lead, a product operations manager, and in one case an HR team.


Community Health System is the clearest example. The not-for-profit healthcare network serving California's central San Joaquin Valley runs an employee engagement survey across 250 departments, and the team that runs the analysis is its Organizational Development team. Not a data function. An HR function. They[produced 250 standardized one-page department reports in three days](https://getthematic.com/insights/community-health-systems-actionable-insights) , cutting analysis time by 67% and saving over 160 hours per survey cycle. The division of labor is worth noting: Thematic clustered the comments into themes and generated the summaries, and the Organizational Development team handled the judgment calls.


At Greyhound, the bus transportation network operating across the United States, Canada and Mexico, the before state was one person. "Previously, only one person, myself, would manually analyze the feedback. It was about 80% of my job," said Matthew Schoolfield, Senior Customer Insights Analyst. After Thematic, work that used to take two to three weeks took ten minutes, and station managers began checking the dashboards themselves.


The sharpest version of this comes from a marketing director rather than an analyst, describing what she can now do with net promoter score (NPS) data unaided. "Thematic makes me look a lot more data-savvy than perhaps I am," said[Emma Glazer, marketing director at DoorDash](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-doordash-builds-customer-understanding) . "I can whip up a very quick waterfall chart showing the impacts of themes on NPS from one month or quarter to another."


## What would a data scientist actually cost you?


This is where the question stops being abstract. US government labor data answers it precisely.


The median annual wage for data scientists was $120,230 in May 2025, according to the[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/math/data-scientists.htm) . Employment is projected to grow 35% from 2025 to 2035, which makes it the[third fastest-growing occupation](https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/fastest-growing-occupations.htm) the BLS tracks. There were about 275,600 data scientists in the United States in 2025, with roughly 24,800 openings projected each year.


Now the comparison nobody makes.[Market research analysts](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/market-research-analysts.htm) , whose job the BLS describes as gathering and analyzing data on consumers and competitors, had a median wage of $78,760 in May 2025. There were about 952,700 of them, with roughly 82,000 openings a year.


**Data scientists** **Market research analysts**

There are 3.5 times more market research analysts than data scientists. They cost about 35% less. More than three times as many come onto the market each year. And analyzing consumer data is already their job description. Staffing a feedback program with a data scientist means competing in the hardest hiring market the BLS tracks, for a skill set the work doesn't call for.


## When do you genuinely need a data scientist?


Three cases. Pretending otherwise would be selling.


1. **You are building it yourself.** Then you need data scientists, engineers, and someone to own the thing permanently, at[what it costs to build one in-house](https://getthematic.com/insights/cost-to-build-an-ai-feedback-analytics-platform) .[MIT NANDA's 2025 study of enterprise AI](https://mlq.ai/media/quarterly_decks/v0.1_State_of_AI_in_Business_2025_Report.pdf) found that within its sample of 52 organizations, externally partnered tools reached deployment about 67% of the time against about 33% for internally built ones. The report is explicit that this reflects its own interview sample and may not represent broader market patterns, so treat it as directional. The mechanism behind it is better evidenced: a[systematic review of 48 papers on concept drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02901) in text streams found that models degrade in performance over time as data distributions shift, and that labeling remained costly and still required a human in the loop.
2. **You need bespoke statistical modeling.** Custom driver analysis beyond what the platform computes, or a model tailored to a scoring problem nobody else has.
3. **You need unusual data engineering.** Joining feedback to financial systems in ways the standard connectors do not cover.


None of those is operating the platform. They're building, extending, or plumbing around it.


One statistic to distrust while you're here. The claim that data scientists spend 80% of their time cleaning data gets repeated constantly and isn't well sourced.[Leigh Dodds traced the citation chain](https://blog.ldodds.com/2020/01/31/do-data-scientists-spend-80-of-their-time-cleaning-data-turns-out-no/) back through IBM marketing to a 2016 vendor survey and concluded the figure doesn't hold up. The underlying surveys disagree with each other and with the headline.


## How does Thematic keep the operator non-technical?


**Themes are discovered, not engineered.** Thematic uses self-supervised AI pre-trained on customer feedback language, so themes emerge from the data rather than from a taxonomy someone has to design first. There's no labeling phase and no taxonomy workshop to staff.


**Refinement is a visual editor, not a model.** Thematic's own line on this is blunt: "You don't need to be a data scientist. If you can move files into folders on your computer, you can use our Themes Editor." Refinement is optional, and Thematic reports[80% to 90% theme accuracy](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-accurate-is-thematic) before any human touches it.


**Questions get asked in plain English.**[Agentic Answers](https://getthematic.com/product/agentic-answers) takes plain-language questions with no query syntax, and it's available with no setup or configuration. That's what lets a marketing director build a waterfall chart without booking an analyst's afternoon.


**The skill the human needs is business context, not statistics.** This matters, because "no data scientist required" is not the same as "no human judgment required". Someone still has to decide whether a theme matches how the business thinks, and whether a suggestion fits the analytical goal. That's domain knowledge. It's the thing your CX team already has and a newly hired data scientist wouldn't. It is also why[designing review that actually catches errors](https://getthematic.com/insights/human-review-ai-insights-automation-bias) matters more than who holds the login.


## A buyer's checklist


1. **Who on your team would log in on Monday?** If you can't name the person, the problem is ownership, not skills.
2. **Ask the vendor to have a non-technical person refine a theme, live.** Not a slide about it. If it needs a specialist, you've just found your ongoing cost.
3. **Ask who rewrites the logic when a new issue appears.** If the answer is a data engineer with a backlog, your insights cadence is that backlog.
4. **Ask what happens on day one with no refinement at all.** A platform that's useful before anyone tunes it is a platform your team can actually run.
5. **Ask how someone outside the insights team gets an answer.** If every question routes through one analyst, you've rebuilt the bottleneck.


## The short answer


No, you don't need a data scientist to run an AI feedback analytics platform you've bought. You need someone who knows your customers and your business, which is usually an insights analyst or a CX manager you already employ. Thematic is built for that person: themes discovered automatically, refinement through a visual editor, and questions asked in plain English.


You need a data scientist to build one. That's the case for not building one.


Here's the test. Ask a vendor to run your own feedback through their platform, then have someone from your CX team, not theirs, find one insight in it unaided. If that works, the staffing question is answered.
